chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: Another way to visualize and evaluate the accuracy of a regression algorithm

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: is to look at the relationship between predicted and

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: actual values of our dependent variable y.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: Here's what I mean.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: Query our model, the one that we trained on training data,

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: with x test, our testing data set.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: The output of that query is a new vector of y values, y predict.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: So based on this x test data, our model predicts this y predict data.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: We can now compare what we know to be the correct or

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: true data in y test with what our prediction was.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: So this pair would appear somewhere on this chart, say here.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: So its value along the horizontal axis here is what the prediction was,

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: and along the vertical axis was what the ground truth is.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: So we can plot these pairs all the way through our data.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: Now if this scatter plot is arranged in approximately a nice line like this,

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: that means we've got a pretty good prediction algorithm.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: On the other hand, if they're not aligned so well, and

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: they look sort of like a shotgun blast, our learner is not so good.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: We can measure this property quantitatively using something called correlation.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: You can use the numpy function core coif to measure the correlation

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: between y test and y predict.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: You'll get an answer somewhere between negative 1 and positive 1,

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: where positive 1 means they're strongly correlated.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: Negative 1 means they're inversely correlated.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: And 0 means there's essentially no correlation at all between them.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: One thing to point out here is that correlation isn't the slope of this line.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: Lots of people think that's what it is.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: Correlation has to do with how well aligned the points are with the line that we fit.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: So if it's a nice oval that fits close to that line, we usually have a high correlation.

chunks.title: Metric 2  Correlation
chunks.text: If it's a big round thing, we've got poor correlation.

text: Another way to visualize and evaluate the accuracy of a regression algorithm is to look at the relationship between predicted and actual values of our dependent variable y. Here's what I mean. Query our model, the one that we trained on training data, with x test, our testing data set. The output of that query is a new vector of y values, y predict. So based on this x test data, our model predicts this y predict data. We can now compare what we know to be the correct or true data in y test with what our prediction was. So this pair would appear somewhere on this chart, say here. So its value along the horizontal axis here is what the prediction was, and along the vertical axis was what the ground truth is. So we can plot these pairs all the way through our data. Now if this scatter plot is arranged in approximately a nice line like this, that means we've got a pretty good prediction algorithm. On the other hand, if they're not aligned so well, and they look sort of like a shotgun blast, our learner is not so good. We can measure this property quantitatively using something called correlation. You can use the numpy function core coif to measure the correlation between y test and y predict. You'll get an answer somewhere between negative 1 and positive 1, where positive 1 means they're strongly correlated. Negative 1 means they're inversely correlated. And 0 means there's essentially no correlation at all between them. One thing to point out here is that correlation isn't the slope of this line. Lots of people think that's what it is. Correlation has to do with how well aligned the points are with the line that we fit. So if it's a nice oval that fits close to that line, we usually have a high correlation. If it's a big round thing, we've got poor correlation.
